Module 09 / Physics 2

Induction: change in flux, not merely the presence of a magnet

Changing flux, Lenz law, induced fields, transformers, and RL circuits.

Topics in this module
Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing fluxFaraday's law and the full product derivativeLenz's law with four direction casesMotional emf from two derivationsGenerators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currentsMutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energyRL growth, decay, and arbitrary initial currentFlux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experimentFull Faraday and transformer solutionsSolve Lenz's law and motional-emf cases step by stepThe missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fieldsMutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decayWorked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

An induced emf can exist without a closed conducting circuit. A closed path is required for the ordinary induced current examples. A stationary loop in a time-varying magnetic field can have emf even when no wire moves. Conversely, motion that leaves the relevant flux unchanged need not produce a net loop emf.

Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing flux

ΦB=∫B⋅dA,ΦB=BAcos⁡θ for uniform B.\Phi_B=\int\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A,\quad \Phi_B=BA\cos\theta\ \text{for uniform }B.ΦB​=∫B⋅dA,ΦB​=BAcosθ for uniform B.

The angle is between B and the AREA NORMAL. If a problem gives the angle to the plane, use the complementary angle. One weber is one T⋅m2T \cdot m^{2}T⋅m2. A field perpendicular to the plane produces maximum flux magnitude; a field parallel to the plane produces zero flux.

If B occupies only an overlap area, integrate over that region. Primary p. 10 has flux BA2BA_{2}BA2​, not BA1BA_{1}BA1​, when the field is confined to the smaller perpendicular overlap area A2A_{2}A2​. Treat “zero outside the field region” explicitly.

Faraday's law and the full product derivative

Faraday's law is a fundamental induction law in this course. For N turns linking the same flux, E=−NdΦBdt\mathcal{E} = - \frac{N d\Phi B}{dt}E=−dtNdΦB​. For nonidentical linked fluxes, sum the flux linkages instead of assuming NΦN\PhiNΦ. The finite average magnitude is N∣ΔΦ∣Δt\frac{N \left| \Delta \Phi \right|}{\Delta t}ΔtN∣ΔΦ∣​; it equals the instantaneous value only for a constant rate during the interval.

E=−N(Acos⁡θdBdt+Bcos⁡θdAdt−BAsin⁡θdθdt).\mathcal E=-N\left(A\cos\theta\frac{dB}{dt}+B\cos\theta\frac{dA}{dt}-BA\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right).E=−N(AcosθdtdB​+BcosθdtdA​−BAsinθdtdθ​).

This product-rule expression covers changing field strength, changing area, changing orientation, and simultaneous changes. Set only the quantities explicitly held constant to zero.

Lenz's law with four direction cases

Choose the external field direction, then determine whether its flux increases or decreases. The induced field OPPOSES THE CHANGE, not necessarily the external field. Use the right-hand grip rule to convert the required induced field into conventional current.

External flux seen by the observer Required induced field Induced current as seen by that observer
Into page, increasing Out of page Counterclockwise
Into page, decreasing Into page Clockwise
Out of page, increasing Into page Clockwise
Out of page, decreasing Out of page Counterclockwise

Primary p. 28 prints a decreasing inward-field example with the wrong outward induced field. For its stated inward and decreasing flux, the correction is inward induced field and clockwise current. Always check the actual loop position and arrow before applying a memorized wire-direction answer.

Motional emf from two derivations

Flux derivation. A rod of length ℓ slides distance dx in a perpendicular uniform B. The loop's area change is dA=ℓdxdA = \ell dxdA=ℓdx, so ∣E∣=Bℓ(dxdt)=Bℓv\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = B \ell \left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right) = B \ell v∣E∣=Bℓ(dtdx​)=Bℓv.

Charge-force derivation. Charges in an open moving rod redistribute until qE balances the magnetic qvB. Thus E=vBE = vBE=vB, and voltage magnitude Eℓ=BℓvE \ell = B \ell vEℓ=Bℓv. The general expression is ∫(v×B)⋅dl\int \left( v \times B \right) \cdot dl∫(v×B)⋅dl; the product Bℓv needs the stated perpendicular geometry.

For a sliding rod in a closed resistance R: I=BℓvRI = \frac{B \ell v}{R}I=RBℓv​. Magnetic drag magnitude is F=IℓB=B2ℓ2vRF = I \ell B = \frac{B^{2} \ell^{2} v}{R}F=IℓB=RB2ℓ2v​. Required mechanical power at constant speed is Fv=I2RFv = I^{2} RFv=I2R, which verifies energy conservation.

Worked example — primary p. 35. Speed 1000 kmh=277.778 ms\frac{1000\,\mathrm{km}}{h} = 277.778\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}h1000km​=277.778sm​. A 70 m70\,\mathrm{m}70m wingspan moving perpendicular to a nearly vertical 5.0×10−5 T5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}5.0×10−5T field develops about 0.9722 V0.9722\,\mathrm{V}0.9722V between tips. Which tip is positive depends on the velocity and field vector directions.

Generators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currents

For a rigid rotating N-turn coil, Φ=BAcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)Φ=BAcos(ωt+ϕ). Differentiate to derive E(t)=NBAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)\mathcal{E} \left( t \right) = NBA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)E(t)=NBAωsin(ωt+ϕ), with peak NBAωNBA\omegaNBAω. A GENERATOR converts mechanical input into electrical output. Primary p. 14 reverses that conversion in its wording; it describes motor action instead. A moving-coil microphone converts mechanical vibration into an electrical signal.

An ideal transformer links both windings to the same changing core flux. Dividing their Faraday equations gives VsVp=NsNp\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}Vp​Vs​​=Np​Ns​​. With ideal power conservation, VpIp=VsIsV_{p} I_{p} = V_{s} I_{s}Vp​Ip​=Vs​Is​ and IsIp=NpNs\frac{I_{s}}{I_{p}} = \frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}Ip​Is​​=Ns​Np​​. These are compatible AC magnitudes, usually rms values. A transformer does not directly convert AC into DC; a rectifier and other power-supply stages are required.

Worked example — primary p. 19. Ideal 120 V120\,\mathrm{V}120V to 9 V9\,\mathrm{V}9V AC, Ns=30N_{s} = 30Ns​=30, Is=0.400 AI_{s} = 0.400\,\mathrm{A}Is​=0.400A gives Np=400N_{p} = 400Np​=400 turns, output power: 3.6 W3.6\,\mathrm{W}3.6W, and input current: 0.030 A0.030\,\mathrm{A}0.030A. The slide's description of 9 V9\,\mathrm{V}9V DC includes an implicit rectifier; the transformer equations alone address the AC stage.

Eddy currents circulate in bulk conductors. Their opposing magnetic effects can slow moving metal. Energy becomes heat. A changing current in one coil can induce emf in a nearby coil even without a conducting connection between them.

Mutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energy

Define mutual inductance through E2=−MdI1dt\mathcal{E}_{2} = - \frac{M dI_{1}}{dt}E2​=−dtMdI1​​. For a linear coil, flux linkage NΦ=LIN\Phi = LINΦ=LI, giving Eself=−LdIdt\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - \frac{L dI}{dt}Eself​=−dtLdI​. L and M have units henry: V⋅sA=Ω⋅s\frac{V \cdot s}{A} = \Omega \cdot sAV⋅s​=Ω⋅s. Constant permeability and fixed geometry are part of the simple constant-L model.

For an ideal long solenoid, B=μNIℓB = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}B=ℓμNI​. Flux per turn is BA. Therefore L=NΦI=μN2AℓL = \frac{N\Phi}{I} = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}L=INΦ​=ℓμN2A​. Derive stored energy by P=LI(dIdt)P = LI \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)P=LI(dtdI​) and integrate: U=∫0ILidi=LI22U = \int_{0} ᴵ Li di = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}U=∫0I​Lidi=2LI2​. Inductors resist a CHANGE in current; they do not simply “oppose current” in every situation.

Substitute L=μN2AℓL = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}L=ℓμN2A​ into U=LI22U = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}U=2LI2​ and replace NIℓ\frac{NI}{\ell}ℓNI​ with Bμ\frac{B}{\mu}μB​. This gives U=B2Aℓ(2μ)U = \frac{B^{2} A \ell}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}U=(2μ)B2Aℓ​. Divide by the solenoid's internal field volume Aℓ to get magnetic energy density uB=B2(2μ)u_{B} = \frac{B^{2}}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}uB​=(2μ)B2​. Compare the electric result uE=εE22u_{E} = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2}uE​=2εE2​. Both formulas assume the specified linear material model.

KVL for an ideal L in series with total R gives E=L(dIdt)+RI\mathcal{E} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right) + RIE=L(dtdI​)+RI. Separate and integrate with I(0)=0I \left( 0 \right) = 0I(0)=0:

I(t)=ER(1−e−tR/L),τRL=L/R.I(t)=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}(1-e^{-tR/L}),\quad \tau_{RL}=L/R.I(t)=RE​(1−e−tR/L),τRL​=L/R.

After removing the source while retaining a closed R–L path, I=I0exp⁡(−tRL)I = I_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t R}{L} \right)I=I0​exp(−LtR​). More generally I(t)=If+(I0−If)e−t/τI(t)=I_f+(I_0-I_f)e^{-t/\tau}I(t)=If​+(I0​−If​)e−t/τ. Inductor current is continuous in this ideal finite-voltage model. At DC steady state, an ideal inductor has zero voltage; real winding resistance remains.

For fraction f of final growth, t=−(LR)ln⁡(1−f)t = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln \left( 1 - f \right)t=−(RL​)ln(1−f). For remaining decay fraction f, t=−(LR)ln⁡ft = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln ft=−(RL​)lnf. RC increases its time constant with R; RL decreases its time constant with R. Do not interchange them.

Switching check. A source-free decay needs a closed path. Opening the only path does not make a real inductor's current disappear without consequence. Its induced voltage can become large and cause a spark or flow through a protection component. The simple exponential requires a valid R–L discharge path.

Flux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experiment

Starting and stopping the primary-coil current — primary pp. 5–7. A steady primary current produces a steady field. A stationary secondary loop then has no transformer emf from that constant flux. Starting or stopping the primary current changes the shared flux and produces a secondary emf. The two coils need no conducting connection for this energy transfer.

Flux sign convention. Choose a surface normal first. A field component along that normal gives positive flux; the opposite component gives negative flux. Couple the positive loop direction to the normal by the right-hand grip rule. The Faraday minus sign then has a precise directional meaning.

Worked solution↳

  3. Reverse the surface normal to reverse the signed flux.

Check. BA1BA_{1}BA1​ would incorrectly assign a nonzero field to the whole loop interior. The relevant area is the area where field actually passes through the chosen surface.

Full Faraday and transformer solutions

Derivation∴

The AC generator waveform and rotation units

Source starting point: Primary p. 14. Let a rigid N-turn coil of area A rotate at constant angular speed ω\omegaω in a uniform field. Let θ\thetaθ be the angle between the area normal and B.

  1. Write θ(t)=ωt+ϕ\theta \left( t \right) = \omega t + \phiθ(t)=ωt+ϕ, with angles in radians.
  2. Write the flux per turn as Φ=BAcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)Φ=BAcos(ωt+ϕ).
  3. Differentiate the cosine: dΦdt=−BAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = - BA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)dtdΦ​=−BAωsin(ωt+ϕ).
  4. Apply Faraday's minus sign and multiply by N.
E(t)=NBAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ),Epeak=NBAω,ω=2πf.\mathcal E(t)=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi), \qquad \mathcal E_{peak}=NBA\omega, \qquad \omega=2\pi f.E(t)=NBAωsin(ωt+ϕ),Epeak​=NBAω,ω=2πf.

At maximum flux, the instantaneous flux slope and emf are zero. When the flux passes through zero during this rotation, the emf magnitude reaches its peak. Mechanical rotation supplies the electrical output energy. Do not substitute rotation frequency f in hertz directly for ω\omegaω in radians per second.

Transformer turns and current ratios

Sources: Primary pp. 16–19. Assume ideal coupling, a common changing core flux per turn, and negligible losses.

  1. Write the induced-voltage magnitudes Vp=Np∣dΦdt∣V_{p} = N_{p} \left| \frac{d\Phi}{dt} \right|Vp​=Np​​dtdΦ​​ and Vs=Ns∣dΦdt∣V_{s} = N_{s} \left| \frac{d\Phi}{dt} \right|Vs​=Ns​​dtdΦ​​.
  2. Divide to cancel the common flux-change rate.
  3. Use ideal average-power conservation for matching AC quantities.
VsVp=NsNp,VpIp=VsIs,IsIp=NpNs.\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p},\qquad V_pI_p=V_sI_s,\qquad \frac{I_s}{I_p}=\frac{N_p}{N_s}.Vp​Vs​​=Np​Ns​​,Vp​Ip​=Vs​Is​,Ip​Is​​=Ns​Np​​.

A step-up transformer increases voltage and decreases current for the same ideal transferred power. A step-down transformer does the reverse. Current does not travel across the insulation from one winding into the other. The changing magnetic field couples the circuits.

Source: Primary p. 35. Given: Speed 1000 kmh\frac{1000\,\mathrm{km}}{h}h1000km​, vertical B=5.0×10−5 TB = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}B=5.0×10−5T, and wingspan 70 m70\,\mathrm{m}70m. Use the stated perpendicular geometry.

  2. Calculate ∣ΔV∣=Bℓv=(5.0×10−5)(70)(277.778)=0.972222 V\begin{aligned}\left| \Delta V \right| &= B \ell v \\&= \left( 5.0 \times 10^{-5} \right) \left( 70 \right) \left( 277.778 \right) \\&= 0.972222\,\mathrm{V}\end{aligned}∣ΔV∣​=Bℓv=(5.0×10−5)(70)(277.778)=0.972222V​

Geometry check. The numerical statement gives a magnitude but does not fully identify a compass heading and field sign. Do not invent a left-wing or right-wing polarity without those directions.

The missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fields

Sources: Primary objectives on p. 23 and discussion on p. 34. A changing magnetic flux creates a circulating electric field. It can act on a charge initially at rest. A conducting wire is not required for the electric field to exist.

For electrostatics, a single-valued scalar potential gives E=−∇VE = - \nabla VE=−∇V and ∮E⋅dl=0\oint E \cdot dl = 0∮E⋅dl=0. In induction, the closed-loop integral can be nonzero:

∮E⋅dl=−dΦBdt.\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.∮E⋅dl=−dtdΦB​​.

The E=vBE = vBE=vB inside a moving open rod instead describes charge separation that balances qv×Bqv \times Bqv×B in that rod. It is not a universal formula for the circulating field around every changing magnetic field.

Derivation∴

Induced field inside and outside a circular changing-field region

This labeled extension develops the source objective. Let uniform B(t) point along +z inside radius a and be zero outside. Choose counterclockwise circulation as positive.

  1. By cylindrical symmetry, E is tangent to a centered circle and has constant magnitude along it.
  2. The circulation is Eϕ(2πr)E\phi \left( 2 \pi r \right)Eϕ(2πr).
  3. For r≤ar \le ar≤a, the enclosed magnetic flux is πr2B\pi r^{2} Bπr2B.
  4. For r≥ar \ge ar≥a, the enclosed magnetic flux is πa2B\pi a^{2} Bπa2B.
  5. Apply Faraday's law and solve each region separately.
Eϕ(r)={−r2dBdt,r≤a,−a22rdBdt,r≥a.E_\phi(r)=\begin{cases} -\dfrac r2\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\le a,\\[6pt] -\dfrac{a^2}{2r}\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\ge a. \end{cases}Eϕ​(r)=⎩⎨⎧​−2r​dtdB​,−2ra2​dtdB​,​r≤a,r≥a.​

Checks. Both expressions agree at r=ar = ar=a. E tends to zero at the center. Outside, E can remain nonzero even where the local magnetic field is zero, because the loop encloses changing flux. For increasing +z flux, EϕE\phiEϕ is negative, so the circulation is clockwise.

Mutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decay

Derivation∴

Derive self-inductance from flux linkage

Sources: Primary pp. 37–41. For a linear coil, the total linkage is Λ=NΦ=LI\Lambda = N\Phi = LIΛ=NΦ=LI. If L is constant, differentiation gives dΛdt=L(dIdt)\frac{d \Lambda}{dt} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)dtdΛ​=L(dtdI​). Faraday's law therefore gives Eself=−L(dIdt)\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)Eself​=−L(dtdI​).

For a long solenoid, substitute B=μNIℓB = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}B=ℓμNI​ into Φ=BA\Phi = BAΦ=BA:

L=NΦI=N(μNI/ℓ)AI=μN2Aℓ.L=\frac{N\Phi}{I} =\frac{N(\mu NI/\ell)A}{I} =\frac{\mu N^2A}{\ell}.L=INΦ​=IN(μNI/ℓ)A​=ℓμN2A​.

For mutual inductance, use Λ2=N2Φ21=MI1\Lambda_{2} = N_{2} \Phi_{21} = MI_{1}Λ2​=N2​Φ21​=MI1​, so E2=−M(dI1dt)\mathcal{E}_{2} = - M \left( \frac{dI_{1}}{dt} \right)E2​=−M(dtdI1​​) for constant geometry and a linear material. A steady current gives no induced emf from these constant-linkage terms.

Worked solution↳

Interpret a mutual- or self-induced emf measurement

Labeled extension of primary pp. 38–39. Let M=0.040 HM = 0.040\,\mathrm{H}M=0.040H and let primary current rise by 2.0 A2.0\,\mathrm{A}2.0A in 0.010 s0.010\,\mathrm{s}0.010s.

  2. Calculate the secondary emf magnitude: ∣E2∣=M∣ΔIΔt∣=8.0 V\left| \mathcal{E}_{2} \right| = M \left| \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \right| = 8.0\,\mathrm{V}∣E2​∣=M​ΔtΔI​​=8.0V.
  3. Set its polarity with the chosen winding directions and Lenz's law.

For a self-inductor L=0.20 HL = 0.20\,\mathrm{H}L=0.20H whose current rises by 3.0 A3.0\,\mathrm{A}3.0A in 0.050 s0.050\,\mathrm{s}0.050s, the average opposing-emf magnitude is 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V. The negative sign describes opposition to the current change. It does not mean the inductance is negative.

RL decay and the fraction-of-current time

Sources: Primary pp. 42–44. Remove the source while retaining a closed series R–L path. Choose the continuing current as positive.

  1. Write the loop equation L(dIdt)+RI=0L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right) + RI = 0L(dtdI​)+RI=0.

ln⁡II0=−RLt⇒I=I0e−tR/L,t=LRln⁡I0I.\ln\frac{I}{I_0}=-\frac{R}{L}t \Rightarrow I=I_0e^{-tR/L}, \qquad t=\frac LR\ln\frac{I_0}{I}.lnI0​I​=−LR​t⇒I=I0​e−tR/L,t=RL​lnII0​​.

The initial magnetic energy, 12LI02\tfrac{1}{2} LI_{0}^{2}21​LI02​, becomes resistor heating during an ideal source-free decay. The current remains continuous through switching when the circuit supplies a finite-voltage discharge path.

Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: Zero flux does not mean zero emf

A rigid loop rotates at constant angular speed in a uniform magnetic field. At one instant its magnetic flux is zero.

The rotating-loop model compares instantaneous flux with induced emf when the flux is zero.

  1. Write the flux.
Φ=BAcos⁡(ωt)\Phi=BA\cos(\omega t)Φ=BAcos(ωt)
  1. Differentiate it.
E=−NdΦdt=NBAωsin⁡(ωt)\mathcal E=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)E=−NdtdΦ​=NBAωsin(ωt)
  1. Check the zero-flux orientation.
cos⁡(ωt)=0 ⇒ ∣sin⁡(ωt)∣=1\cos(\omega t)=0\ \Rightarrow\ |\sin(\omega t)|=1cos(ωt)=0 ⇒ ∣sin(ωt)∣=1
  1. Keep the distinction. The field, area, or orientation can change the flux.

Result: Yes. For sinusoidal flux, its magnitude is maximum when flux crosses zero.

Worked application 2: Lenz direction for a weakening field

A conducting loop lies in the page. A uniform external magnetic field points out of the page and decreases in magnitude.

Lenz’s law determines the induced conventional-current direction, viewed from the front, as the outward field decreases.

  1. Identify the change. Outward flux is decreasing.

  2. Oppose that change. The induced field must point outward.

  3. Apply the loop right-hand rule. An outward thumb gives counterclockwise curled fingers.

  4. Check the wording. The induced field opposes the change, rather than always opposing the external field.

Result: Counterclockwise.

Worked application 3: The same initial and final flux

The magnetic flux through a fixed N-turn coil changes and later returns to its initial value.

Faraday’s law determines the time integral of the induced emf over the entire interval when the initial flux returns.

  1. Start from Faraday’s law.
E=−N dΦ/dt\mathcal E=-N\,d\Phi/dtE=−NdΦ/dt
  1. Integrate with a fixed orientation.
∫titfE dt=−N(Φf−Φi)\int_{t_i}^{t_f}\mathcal E\,dt=-N(\Phi_f-\Phi_i)∫ti​tf​​Edt=−N(Φf​−Φi​)
  1. Use the equal endpoint values.
Φf=Φi ⇒ ∫E dt=0\Phi_f=\Phi_i\ \Rightarrow\ \int\mathcal E\,dt=0Φf​=Φi​ ⇒ ∫Edt=0
  1. Avoid an extra conclusion. The emf can be nonzero during parts of the interval.

Result: It is zero: ∫E dt=0\int\mathcal E\,dt=0∫Edt=0.

Worked application 4: A transformer after the DC transient

A transformer primary has nonzero winding resistance. A DC source has been connected long enough for its current and core flux to become constant. Ignore leakage and saturation.

The constant final core flux determines the secondary induced emf after the DC transient ends.

  1. Identify the stated steady condition. After the transient, the current and flux are constant.

  2. Apply Faraday’s law to the secondary.

Es=−Ns dΦ/dt\mathcal E_s=-N_s\,d\Phi/dtEs​=−Ns​dΦ/dt
  1. Use the zero derivative.
dΦ/dt=0 ⇒ Es=0d\Phi/dt=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mathcal E_s=0dΦ/dt=0 ⇒ Es​=0
  1. Separate switching from steady operation. Connection and disconnection can produce transient secondary emf.

Result: Zero.

Worked application 5: An inductor starts to discharge

An inductor carrying current is disconnected from its source and connected into a closed loop with a finite resistor.

Inductor-current continuity determines the current immediately after switching into the closed resistor loop.

  1. Use the inductor relation.
VL=L di/dtV_L=L\,di/dtVL​=Ldi/dt
  1. Write the source-free loop equation.
L di/dt+Ri=0L\,di/dt+Ri=0Ldi/dt+Ri=0
  1. Use current continuity.
i(t)=I0e−Rt/L,i(0+)=I0i(t)=I_0e^{-Rt/L},\quad i(0^+)=I_0i(t)=I0​e−Rt/L,i(0+)=I0​
  1. Check energy transfer. The resistor dissipates the magnetic energy initially stored in the inductor.

Result: Current starts from its previous value and then decays continuously.

Worked application 6: Both field and area change

A 100-turn coil has a uniform perpendicular field B(t)=(0.20+0.10t) TB(t)=(0.20+0.10t)\,\mathrm TB(t)=(0.20+0.10t)T and area A(t)=(0.030−0.002t) m2A(t)=(0.030-0.002t)\,\mathrm{m^2}A(t)=(0.030−0.002t)m2, with t in seconds. Choose positive flux along the field and positive emf around its right-hand-rule contour. The calculation determines the signed induced emf at t=2.0 st=2.0\,\mathrm st=2.0s.

  1. Use flux per turn.
Φ(t)=B(t)A(t)\Phi(t)=B(t)A(t)Φ(t)=B(t)A(t)
  1. Differentiate both changing factors.
E=−N[A dB/dt+B dA/dt]\mathcal E=-N[A\,dB/dt+B\,dA/dt]E=−N[AdB/dt+BdA/dt]
  1. Evaluate the instantaneous quantities.
B(2)=0.40 T,A(2)=0.026 m2B(2)=0.40\,\mathrm T,\quad A(2)=0.026\,\mathrm{m^2}B(2)=0.40T,A(2)=0.026m2
  1. Substitute both contributions.
E=−100[(0.026)(0.10)+(0.40)(−0.002)]=−0.180 V\mathcal E=-100[(0.026)(0.10)+(0.40)(-0.002)]=-0.180\,\mathrm VE=−100[(0.026)(0.10)+(0.40)(−0.002)]=−0.180V

  1. Interpret the sign. Field growth dominates area shrinkage, so positive flux increases and the emf acts in the negative contour direction.

  2. State the result.

−0.18 V-0.18\,\mathrm V−0.18V

Result: −0.18 V-0.18\,\mathrm V−0.18V

Worked application 7: Emf of a rotating coil

A 100-turn coil of area 0.010 m² rotates in a uniform 0.20 T field at 50 rad/s. Its normal makes an increasing angle of 30° with the field. The calculation determines the instantaneous induced emf magnitude.

  1. Write the angle-dependent flux.
Φ=BAcos⁡θ\Phi=BA\cos\thetaΦ=BAcosθ
  1. Differentiate using angular speed.
∣E∣=NBAω∣sin⁡θ∣|\mathcal E|=NBA\omega|\sin\theta|∣E∣=NBAω∣sinθ∣

∣E∣=(100)(0.20)(0.010)(50)sin⁡30∘=5.00 V|\mathcal E|=(100)(0.20)(0.010)(50)\sin30^\circ=5.00\,\mathrm V∣E∣=(100)(0.20)(0.010)(50)sin30∘=5.00V

  1. Check the angle. Use the angle to the normal. The maximum occurs at a normal angle of 90°.

  2. State the result.

5 V5\,\mathrm V5V

Result: 5 V5\,\mathrm V5V

Worked application 14: An RL circuit with initial current · the instantaneous resistor heating power

A series RL loop has resistance 6 Ω, inductance 3 H, and ideal source 12 V. Just before a switch establishes this loop, the inductor current is 0.3 A in the source-driven positive direction. Worked application 21: Where the inductor energy goes · the current at the stated time

An inductor of 1.8 H initially carries 1.5 A. It discharges into a closed 9 Ω resistor loop with no source. Neglect other losses. Consider time 0.08 s after the decay begins. The current reference follows the initial current. The calculation determines the current at the stated time.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Current decays with time constant L/R. Energy depends on current squared, so it decays twice as fast in the exponential.

  2. Find the current decay.

I=I0e−Rt/L=1.00548 AI=I_0e^{-Rt/L}=1.00548\,\mathrm AI=I0​e−Rt/L=1.00548A
  1. Find the remaining and dissipated energies.
UL=12LI02e−2Rt/L,QR=12LI02−ULU_L=\tfrac12LI_0^2e^{-2Rt/L},\quad Q_R=\tfrac12LI_0^2-U_LUL​=21​LI02​e−2Rt/L,QR​=21​LI02​−UL​
  1. Derive the energy half-time.
e−2Rt1/2/L=1/2 ⇒ t1/2=Lln⁡22Re^{-2Rt_{1/2}/L}=1/2\ \Rightarrow\ t_{1/2}=\frac{L\ln2}{2R}e−2Rt1/2​/L=1/2 ⇒ t1/2​=2RLln2​
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
I=1.5e−9(0.08)/1.8I=1.5e^{-9(0.08)/1.8}I=1.5e−9(0.08)/1.8

  1. Check the physical result. The current remains in its original direction while its magnitude decays.

  2. State the result.

1.00548 A1.00548\,\mathrm A1.00548A

Result: 1.00548 A1.00548\,\mathrm A1.00548A

Worked application 30: Where the inductor energy goes · model and interpretation

An inductor of 2.4 H initially carries 2 A. It discharges into a closed 12 Ω resistor loop with no source. Neglect other losses. Consider time 0.12 s after the decay begins. The current reference follows the initial current.

The inductor’s stored magnetic energy maintains current while the resistor dissipates energy after source removal.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Current decays with time constant L/R. Energy depends on current squared, so it decays twice as fast in the exponential.

  2. Find the current decay.

I=I0e−Rt/L=1.09762 AI=I_0e^{-Rt/L}=1.09762\,\mathrm AI=I0​e−Rt/L=1.09762A
  1. Find the remaining and dissipated energies.
UL=12LI02e−2Rt/L,QR=12LI02−ULU_L=\tfrac12LI_0^2e^{-2Rt/L},\quad Q_R=\tfrac12LI_0^2-U_LUL​=21​LI02​e−2Rt/L,QR​=21​LI02​−UL​
  1. Derive the energy half-time.
e−2Rt1/2/L=1/2 ⇒ t1/2=Lln⁡22Re^{-2Rt_{1/2}/L}=1/2\ \Rightarrow\ t_{1/2}=\frac{L\ln2}{2R}e−2Rt1/2​/L=1/2 ⇒ t1/2​=2RLln2​
  1. Apply the conclusion. The induced emf opposes the current decrease.

Result: Its changing magnetic field transfers stored energy into the resistor loop.

Worked application 41: A sliding rod opposes a battery · the signed loop current

A conducting rod of length 0.4 m slides at constant speed 4 m/s on ideal rails in a uniform perpendicular field of 0.50 T. Rod, velocity, and field are mutually perpendicular. Its motional emf drives the positive loop direction. A 0.3 V ideal battery opposes that direction. Total circuit resistance is 2.0 Ω. Ignore friction and self-inductance. Define external force positive along the rod velocity; define battery power positive when absorbed. The calculation determines the signed loop current.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Add the signed battery and motional emfs. Current reversal can turn magnetic drag into a magnetic driving force.

  2. Calculate motional emf.

Em=BLv=0.8 V\mathcal E_m=BLv=0.8\,\mathrm VEm​=BLv=0.8V
  1. Apply the signed loop equation.
I=(Em−Eb)/R=0.25 AI=(\mathcal E_m-\mathcal E_b)/R=0.25\,\mathrm AI=(Em​−Eb​)/R=0.25A
  1. Balance the magnetic force at constant speed.
Fext=BLI,Pext=FextvF_{\rm ext}=BLI,\quad P_{\rm ext}=F_{\rm ext}vFext​=BLI,Pext​=Fext​v
  1. Check the power balance.
EmI=I2R+EbI\mathcal E_mI=I^2R+\mathcal E_bIEm​I=I2R+Eb​I
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
I=(0.8−0.3)/2=0.25 AI=(0.8-0.3)/2=0.25\,\mathrm AI=(0.8−0.3)/2=0.25A

  1. Check the physical result. The sign is positive when motional emf wins and negative when the battery wins.

  2. State the result.

0.25 A0.25\,\mathrm A0.25A

Result: 0.25 A0.25\,\mathrm A0.25A

Worked application 45: A sliding rod opposes a battery · model and interpretation

A conducting rod of length 0.4 m slides at constant speed 4 m/s on ideal rails in a uniform perpendicular field of 0.50 T. Rod, velocity, and field are mutually perpendicular. Its motional emf drives the positive loop direction. A 0.3 V ideal battery opposes that direction. Total circuit resistance is 2.0 Ω. Ignore friction and self-inductance. Define external force positive along the rod velocity; define battery power positive when absorbed.

When the battery emf exceeds the motional emf, the constant-speed balance determines the external agent’s braking action.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Add the signed battery and motional emfs. Current reversal can turn magnetic drag into a magnetic driving force.

  2. Calculate motional emf.

Em=BLv=0.8 V\mathcal E_m=BLv=0.8\,\mathrm VEm​=BLv=0.8V
  1. Apply the signed loop equation.
I=(Em−Eb)/R=0.25 AI=(\mathcal E_m-\mathcal E_b)/R=0.25\,\mathrm AI=(Em​−Eb​)/R=0.25A
  1. Balance the magnetic force at constant speed.
Fext=BLI,Pext=FextvF_{\rm ext}=BLI,\quad P_{\rm ext}=F_{\rm ext}vFext​=BLI,Pext​=Fext​v
  1. Check the power balance.
EmI=I2R+EbI\mathcal E_mI=I^2R+\mathcal E_bIEm​I=I2R+Eb​I
  1. Apply the conclusion. The negative signed loop current reverses the magnetic-force direction.

Result: Apply a braking force because current reverses and the magnetic force drives the rod.

Worked application 51: A transformer with stated efficiency · the secondary rms voltage

A transformer operates on sinusoidal AC with primary rms voltage 24 V. It has 100 primary turns and 500 secondary turns. A 240 Ω resistor loads the secondary. Use a model with the ideal turns voltage ratio, unity primary power factor, and total efficiency 0.9. All losses are represented by that efficiency. The calculation determines the secondary rms voltage.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Use the turns ratio for voltage under the stated model. Use efficiency for real input power before converting that power to primary rms current.

  2. Find secondary voltage and current.

Vs=VpNs/Np=120 V,Is=Vs/R=0.5 AV_s=V_pN_s/N_p=120\,\mathrm V,\quad I_s=V_s/R=0.5\,\mathrm AVs​=Vp​Ns​/Np​=120V,Is​=Vs​/R=0.5A
  1. Include efficiency in the power balance.
Pout=VsIs=60 W,Pin=Pout/η=66.6667 WP_{\rm out}=V_sI_s=60\,\mathrm W,\quad P_{\rm in}=P_{\rm out}/\eta=66.6667\,\mathrm WPout​=Vs​Is​=60W,Pin​=Pout​/η=66.6667W
  1. Use the specified unity primary power factor.
Ip=Pin/VpI_p=P_{\rm in}/V_pIp​=Pin​/Vp​
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Vs=24(500/100)=120 VV_s=24(500/100)=120\,\mathrm VVs​=24(500/100)=120V

  1. Check the physical result. The voltage follows the explicitly stated turns-ratio model, not an extra efficiency factor.

  2. State the result.

120 V120\,\mathrm V120V

Result: 120 V120\,\mathrm V120V

Worked application 60: A transformer with stated efficiency · model and interpretation

A transformer operates on sinusoidal AC with primary rms voltage 120 V. It has 300 primary turns and 150 secondary turns. A 30 Ω resistor loads the secondary. Use a model with the ideal turns voltage ratio, unity primary power factor, and total efficiency 0.85. All losses are represented by that efficiency.

The unity primary power factor connects the real input power with the primary rms current.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Use the turns ratio for voltage under the stated model. Use efficiency for real input power before converting that power to primary rms current.

  2. Find secondary voltage and current.

Vs=VpNs/Np=60 V,Is=Vs/R=2 AV_s=V_pN_s/N_p=60\,\mathrm V,\quad I_s=V_s/R=2\,\mathrm AVs​=Vp​Ns​/Np​=60V,Is​=Vs​/R=2A
  1. Include efficiency in the power balance.
Pout=VsIs=120 W,Pin=Pout/η=141.176 WP_{\rm out}=V_sI_s=120\,\mathrm W,\quad P_{\rm in}=P_{\rm out}/\eta=141.176\,\mathrm WPout​=Vs​Is​=120W,Pin​=Pout​/η=141.176W
  1. Use the specified unity primary power factor.
Ip=Pin/VpI_p=P_{\rm in}/V_pIp​=Pin​/Vp​
  1. Apply the conclusion. Efficiency supplies real input power; a power-factor model is also needed to infer rms current.

Result: Otherwise real power is Vp Ip times power factor, so P/V alone would not determine rms current.
